S2.F1.caption: Fig. 1: Model Architecture
citing_paragraphs: Our study builds on Koel-TTS, an encoder-decoder TTS system [3]. The encoder processes linguistic inputs, while the decoder autoregressively predicts discrete acoustic tokens (Figure 1). For audio tokenization we use a 21.5 frames per second, 8-codebook NanoCodec [11]. Koel-TTS predicts all NN codebooks at each timestep in parallel. While efficient, this parallel decoding inherits the limitations discussed above, that is, the intra-frame dependencies are ignored. Consequently, the generated speech suffers from reduced fidelity, which we empirically demonstrate in our experiments (Section 3). To address this, we augment Koel-TTS with an LT that explicitly models intra-frame dependencies, enabling iterative prediction of the codebooks.

Table 2(g) provides a full set of evaluation metrics on LibriTTS. In all reported results, baseline denotes the non-stacked model (1x-stacked) with no LT, parallel-sampled across all codebooks of a single frame. Speeds are reported in Figure 2(f). We next review these results.

Figure 2(e) shows the FDs for unseen speakers (trends for seen speakers are similar). At each stacking factor, the LT-based models have a lower (better) FD than the no-LT (parallel-sampled) model. In fact, remarkably, all LT-based models, at all stacking factors, have a lower FD than all parallel models, even the unstacked one. This result supports the hypothesis that iterative sampling generates a distribution that is closer to the ground truth than parallel sampling.

contextual_paragraphs.html: At a frame stacking factor of 1, SSIMs and MOS estimates for both LT-based models outperform baseline for both seen and unseen speakers. WERs are slightly higher for LT models compared to baseline, but the difference is not statistically significant. Speeds are similar across the three models. Overall, the LT-based models are a better choice at this stacking factor, producing better SSIM, MOS and FD at similar speed. At a frame stacking factor of 2, we start observing major speed benefits from frame stacking. The AR LT is 2.1x faster and the MaskGIT LT 3.1x faster than the unstacked parallel baseline. SSIMs are similar to baseline for seen speakers and nearly as good for unseen speakers. MOS scores are better or within CI of baseline. If we try to parallel-sample from a 2x-stacked model, the sampling starts to degrade substantially, with FDs in particular worsening by 67% for unseen speakers and MOS decreasing. This is not surprising as parallel sampling two frames, rather than one, can only exacerbate the issues with parallel sampling discussed earlier. Overall, even at a stacking factor of 2, the LT-based models are a better choice than the baseline. At a frame stacking factor of 4, there are large speedups of 2.9x (LT) and 5.5x (MaskGIT) vs baseline but with some cost in quality and robustness: SSIMs drop a little for seen speakers but substantially for unseen speakers. WER confidence intervals remain overlapping with baseline. FDs remain better than baseline. MOS for the AR LT remains similar to baseline but for MaskGit there is a significant drop. We attribute this drop to our use of only 3 sampling steps—a constraint likely too severe for sampling 8×4=328\times 4=32 tokens—and expect that relaxing it could mitigate the degradation. Parallel sampling breaks at this stacking factor, with large large degradations in both FD and SSIM. Based on these results, we propose the following practical guidelines:

S3.F2.sf3.caption: (c) SSIM (seen speakers)

contextual_paragraphs.html: We evaluate the model on the same seen and unseen-speaker subsets of LibriTTS [17] as [3], containing 180 utterances each. To assess text adherence, we report the Word Error Rate (WER) computed with the Parakeet-TDT-1.1b ASR model [18]. For Speaker Similarity (SSIM) , we extract speaker embeddings using TitaNet-Large [19] and compute the cosine similarity between the generated and reference (context) audio. Following [20] and others, we compute a Fréchet Distance (FD) in the codec’s 32-dimensional embedding space. We use model-generated frames as the generated distribution and the ground truth LibriTTS codec frames of the same utterances as the real distribution. This metric measures how closely the distribution of generated and real codec frames match, capturing both fidelity and diversity. If a sampling method yields implausible codebook token combinations, this metric should detect it. We report speech quality using UTMOSv2 [21], a state-of-the-art neural estimator of naturalness mean opinion scores (MOS). Inference speed (i.e., throughput) is reported relative to the baseline’s speed.222To ensure our quality comparisons were fair, the baseline model was designed with 16 decoder layers to match the total layer count (12+4) of the LT models. While this establishes an equitable footing for quality metrics, it slightly inflates speedup figures. A baseline with only 12 layers would be roughly 14% faster, which would proportionally lower the speedup figures we report. Nevertheless, the fundamental conclusion that frame-stacked models offer significant throughput gains remains valid.

Figure 2(e) shows the FDs for unseen speakers (trends for seen speakers are similar). At each stacking factor, the LT-based models have a lower (better) FD than the no-LT (parallel-sampled) model. In fact, remarkably, all LT-based models, at all stacking factors, have a lower FD than all parallel models, even the unstacked one. This result supports the hypothesis that iterative sampling generates a distribution that is closer to the ground truth than parallel sampling.

At a frame stacking factor of 1, SSIMs and MOS estimates for both LT-based models outperform baseline for both seen and unseen speakers. Overall, the LT-based models are a better choice at this stacking factor, producing better SSIM, MOS and FD at similar speed. SSIMs are similar to baseline for seen speakers and nearly as good for unseen speakers. MOS scores are better or within CI of baseline. This is not surprising as parallel sampling two frames, rather than one, can only exacerbate the issues with parallel sampling discussed earlier. Overall, even at a stacking factor of 2, the LT-based models are a better choice than the baseline. contextual_paragraphs.html: In the MaskGIT [12] variant, the LT starts from a fully masked sequence and progressively unmasks it through iterative prediction. The LT is configured with non-causal self-attention. The input sequence is initialized with the hidden state followed by NN mask embeddings. After each forward pass, a subset of predictions is retained and unmasked, and this partially unmasked sequence is fed into the next iteration. After PP iterations, all NN codebooks are decoded. Importantly, PP can be smaller than NN, allowing multiple tokens to be predicted in parallel, thereby speeding up inference and allowing a flexible tradeoff between speed and quality. In addition to its speed benefits, this scheme also enables bidirectional dependency modeling between codebooks in the frame, without constraining decoding to a particular codebook order (unlike the AR LT). The main drawback is that dependencies between codebooks that get unmasked in the same iteration are not captured, i.e. the modeling of the joint probability distribution is approximate, as discussed in [13].

We evaluate the model on the same seen and unseen-speaker subsets of LibriTTS [17] as [3], containing 180 utterances each. To assess text adherence, we report the Word Error Rate (WER) computed with the Parakeet-TDT-1.1b ASR model [18]. For Speaker Similarity (SSIM) , we extract speaker embeddings using TitaNet-Large [19] and compute the cosine similarity between the generated and reference (context) audio. Following [20] and others, we compute a Fréchet Distance (FD) in the codec’s 32-dimensional embedding space. We use model-generated frames as the generated distribution and the ground truth LibriTTS codec frames of the same utterances as the real distribution. This metric measures how closely the distribution of generated and real codec frames match, capturing both fidelity and diversity. If a sampling method yields implausible codebook token combinations, this metric should detect it. We report speech quality using UTMOSv2 [21], a state-of-the-art neural estimator of naturalness mean opinion scores (MOS).
